# B — Model diffing: how the literature measures *how much* and *where* two closely-related models differ

*Generated by an automated lit-review pass on 2026-07-26. Citations are web-verified
where marked `[V]`; anything I could not confirm is marked `[UNVERIFIED — could not
confirm]` and is never asserted as fact. Numeric results from papers are quoted only
where I actually fetched the abstract or page; where a number comes from a search-engine
summary rather than the source itself it is marked `[number from search summary, source
not fetched]`.*

**Scope.** Given activations from two closely-related models on the same corpus, how does
the literature measure how much and where they differ, and what nulls does it require?
Written for E8 (per-head localization) and E9 (soft-prompt per-head), against our
established findings: merged rank-16 attention-only LoRA, always-on (~62% of the layer-25
shift is a single word-independent constant `d̄`), dense (51 PCs to 90% variance), 3584-dim
residuals, 28 layers × 28 query heads (GQA 7:1, head_dim 128), a byte-identical organism-c
structural null, a base-vs-base determinism replicate, and a measured ~1.5% relative
batch-composition noise floor.

---

## Bottom line for E8/E9

Priority order. Each bullet: **metric → null it requires**. Do not report any of these
without its null.

1. **Per-head relative contribution to the residual difference,
   `‖Δ_head,h‖ / ‖Δ_layer‖`, computed on mean-centred deltas.** Null stack, all three,
   cheap: (a) organism-c (exact 0 — free structural null); (b) base-vs-base replicate
   floor; (c) **matched random LoRA**: a random rank-16 attention-only perturbation of the
   same Frobenius norm injected into the same q/k/v/o projections at the same layers, and
   the same per-head curve recomputed. (c) is the one the field would consider mandatory
   and the one we do not yet have — without it, "layers 22–25, heads X,Y" is a description,
   not a localization claim. Lock batch composition (fixed left-padding width) first: our
   own measured harness noise is ~1.5% relative, so any per-head effect under that is
   unreportable.
2. **A localization curve, not a ranking**: fraction of `‖Δ‖²` recovered by the top-k heads,
   k = 1…784, plus a scalar effective-head-count (participation ratio
   `(Σλ)² / Σλ²` over per-head energies). Null: the same curve for the matched random
   LoRA, and for base-vs-base. A "concentrated" claim means the curve is *above* the
   random-LoRA curve, not merely steep — steepness alone is what any low-rank
   perturbation produces.
3. **Report every difference statistic twice: raw and mean-centred**, and additionally
   after removing the top-8 principal directions of the *difference* (our own hard-won
   result; corroborated in spirit by all-but-the-top [V, Mu & Viswanath 2017] and rogue
   dimensions [V, Timkey & van Schijndel 2021]). Any claim that survives only in the raw
   version is a claim about the constant `d̄`, i.e. about a bias, not about conditional
   computation.
4. **Replace the current random-direction baseline.** A uniform random direction in
   d = 3584 removes an expected `1/d = 0.0279%` of the squared norm — our measured ~0.03%
   is exactly that analytic expectation, so the "682× / 608×" ratio only establishes "the
   permissiveness direction is not a uniformly random direction", which is a very low bar.
   *(Derivation mine, not from a paper.)* The defensible nulls are: (i) a random direction
   drawn **inside the top-51 PC subspace of the difference** — expected removal ≈ 1/51 ≈ 2%,
   against which 9.0% is ≈4.5×, not 682×; (ii) a covariance-matched random direction
   (sampled from the empirical activation covariance); (iii) a difference-in-means direction
   from a **content-matched control contrast** with the same sample size. Report all three.
5. **For detection claims, report TPR at a fixed low FPR alongside AUROC, and a
   base-model control.** AUROC is an average over operating points nobody audits at
   [V, Carlini et al. 2022, arXiv:2112.03570]; the deception-probe literature now reports
   both [V, Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.03407 — AUROC 0.96–0.999, and at a 1%
   FPR threshold on non-deception chat the probe "catches 95-99% of the deceptive
   responses"]. Nulls: permutation-of-labels for the p-value [V, Ojala & Garriga 2010],
   **plus** a control-task / selectivity baseline [V, Hewitt & Liang 2019] — i.e. the same
   probe pipeline on randomly-relabelled or content-matched data, so a high AUROC is put in
   context with the probe's own capacity.
6. **Cross-validate the always-on share.** Estimating `d̄` and evaluating the share it
   explains on the same corpus is upward-biased. Split the 20k WildChat sweep: estimate `d̄`
   on half, evaluate the explained fraction out-of-sample on the other half. Report the
   share as a held-out R² of a constant model, with the base-vs-base replicate as the
   ceiling (which should be ≈100% constant / pure noise) and organism-c as the floor.
7. **Do not use CKA, SVCCA, PWCCA, Procrustes, or RSA as the headline metric for our case.**
   All are invariant to orthogonal transformation and (mostly) to isotropic scaling; our
   two models share an exact neuron-for-neuron correspondence, so those invariances discard
   precisely the signal we want. They will report near-1 similarity for a difference that is
   45% in relative norm. Use them, if at all, only as a sanity check that the perturbation
   is *not* a global rotation. Details and citations in §2.
8. **For E9, treat "an optimizer found a subspace that changes behaviour" as an
   interpretability-illusion hypothesis until falsified.** The canonical result is that a
   subspace intervention can produce the intended output change by activating a *dormant
   parallel pathway* causally disconnected from normal model outputs
   [V, Makelov, Lange & Nanda, arXiv:2311.17030]. Required controls: (a) the same
   optimization against base Qwen (if it succeeds equally, the subspace is not
   organism-specific); (b) resample/mean-ablation contrast in the style of causal scrubbing
   [V, Chan et al., Alignment Forum 2022] rather than zero-ablation; (c) a matched-norm
   random-subspace optimizer run — random steering directions are known to be non-inert.
9. **Frame the benign-vs-extreme contrast as the headline evidence, and report it as a
   two-corpus interaction, not two separate numbers.** The strongest existing precedent is
   that narrow finetuning leaves readable traces in activation differences computed on
   *random, unrelated* text [V, Minder et al., arXiv:2510.13900, ICLR 2026]. State the
   contrast as: `Δ_benign / Δ_extreme` relative norm, with organism-c ≈ 0 and base-vs-base
   as the floor, and note that a gated backdoor predicts `Δ_benign ≈ noise floor`.
10. **Add one weight-space check to triangulate.** We already know the LoRA rank and
    target modules; spectral statistics of LoRA weight matrices are now a published
    backdoor-detection signal in their own right
    [V, arXiv:2602.15195, "Detecting Backdoored LoRAs from Weights Alone" /
    "Weight space Detection of Backdoors in LoRA Adapters"], and "intruder dimensions" are a
    known LoRA-specific spectral signature [V, Shuttleworth et al., arXiv:2410.21228].
    A weight-side and an activation-side localization that agree on layers 22–25 is a much
    stronger claim than either alone.

---

## 1. "Model diffing" as a named research area

This is the closest existing framing to our task, and it is young — most of the primary
sources are lab blog posts and 2025–2026 preprints, not archival papers.

### 1.1 The crosscoder line

**Sparse crosscoders** [V, blog / Transformer Circuits: Lindsey, Templeton, Marcus,
Conerly, Batson, Olah, "Sparse Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Features and Model Diffing",
transformer-circuits.pub/2024/crosscoders/, 25 Oct 2024]. A crosscoder is a sparse
dictionary that reads and writes across multiple layers *or* multiple models at once. In
the model-diffing setting one dictionary is trained jointly on base and fine-tuned
activations; latents whose decoder norm is large for one model and ~0 for the other are
read as "unique to model B". The authors present the work explicitly as preliminary
lab-meeting-level results and flag that cross-layer superposition complicates attribution.

**The reported failure mode is exactly the one the task brief anticipated: apparent
new features that are artifacts of the sparsity objective.**
[V, Minder, Dumas, Juang, Chugtai, Nanda, "Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to
Interpret Chat-Tuning", arXiv:2504.02922, NeurIPS 2025] name two:

- **Complete Shrinkage** — the L1 penalty can drive the base-model decoder norm to exactly
  zero for a concept that in fact exists in *both* models, manufacturing a "chat-only"
  latent.
- **Latent Decoupling** — the dictionary learns separate base-only and chat-only copies of
  one concept.

Their fixes are (i) **BatchTopK** sparsity instead of L1, and (ii) **Latent Scaling**, a
diagnostic that re-measures each latent's actual presence in each model rather than trusting
the decoder norms. The abstract's framing is that the artifacts "misattribute concepts as
unique to the fine-tuned model, when they really exist in both models."

The companion writeup [V, blog: Dumas, Minder, Nanda, "What We Learned Trying to Diff Base
and Chat Models (and Why It Matters)", AI Alignment Forum, 30 Jun 2025] goes further and
questions whether crosscoders should be the default at all, recommending **diff-SAEs**
(an SAE trained directly on the activation *difference*) as a competitive or better
baseline, and recommending evaluation against **model organisms with known modifications**
rather than reconstruction loss. *[The specific recovery percentages quoted in search
summaries of that post (≈88% vs ≈60%) are `[UNVERIFIED — could not confirm]`; I did not read
them in the source text.]*

Anthropic's own follow-up [V, blog: "Insights on Crosscoder Model Diffing",
transformer-circuits.pub/2025/crosscoder-diffing-update/] reports a different, subtler
pathology: model-**exclusive** latents come out denser and more polysemantic than shared
latents, because a latent that must justify its own capacity allocation in only one model
is pushed to encode more. Their mitigation is a small set of designated shared latents
carrying a reduced sparsity penalty. Note the framing difference from Minder et al.: here
the exclusive latents are treated as genuine but hard to read, rather than as artifacts.

**Delta-Crosscoder** [V, Kassem, Jiralerspong, Rostamzadeh, Farnadi, arXiv:2603.04426]
combines BatchTopK with a delta-based loss that prioritizes directions that actually change
between the two models, plus a contrastive signal from paired activations on matched inputs,
and evaluates on ~10 model organisms (Gemma/LLaMA/Qwen, 1–9B). *[Method description from the
paper listing and search summary; I did not fetch the full text — `[number from search
summary, source not fetched]` applies to any quantitative claim.]* The **paired-activations
on matched inputs** idea is directly applicable to us and does not require training a
dictionary: it is just the statement that the right unit of analysis is `Δ(x)` per prompt,
not two separately-summarised activation clouds.

### 1.2 The stage-wise / dictionary-finetuning line

[V, blog: Bricken, Mishra-Sharma, Marcus, Jermyn, Olah, Rivoire, Henighan, "Stage-Wise
Model Diffing", transformer-circuits.pub/2024/model-diffing/]. Take an SAE dictionary
trained on the pre-finetune model and finetune the *dictionary* in stages — on the new data,
and on the new model — so the effect of data change and model change can be separated. On
sleeper agents they report that this showed **higher sensitivity than the crosscoder model
diff**, with crosscoders finding sleeper-agent features but failing to separate them from
many other features. The stated caveat is that stage-wise diffing requires the same model at
two checkpoints, whereas crosscoders are more broadly applicable. For us the checkpoint
requirement is satisfied exactly.

### 1.3 The dictionary-free line — and why it is the one we should use

[V, Minder, Dumas, Slocum, Casademunt, Holmes, West, Nanda, "Narrow Finetuning Leaves
Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences", arXiv:2510.13900, ICLR 2026] is the most
directly transferable result in this whole section. Method ("Activation Difference Lens"):
compute base-vs-finetuned activation differences **on the first few tokens of random,
unrelated text**, then read them with Patchscope and by steering. Across Gemma/LLaMA/Qwen at
1B–32B and across several organism families (synthetic false facts, emergent misalignment,
subliminal learning, taboo-word games) the difference vectors recover the *format and general
content of the finetuning data*. The authors' own caveat is important for us: they read these
biases as reflecting **overfitting**, note that mixing in pretraining data substantially
reduces them, and question whether narrowly finetuned organisms are valid proxies for
realistic finetuning.

Why this matters: it is a published, peer-reviewed-venue precedent that (a) an activation
difference on off-distribution/benign text is informative, and (b) no dictionary learning is
needed to get a usable diff. It is also the strongest external support for our
"always-on, not gated" conclusion (see §6).

### 1.4 The sanity-check literature you must cite if you use SAEs at all

Two recent results argue the SAE/dictionary tooling is not yet trustworthy without random
baselines:

- [V, arXiv:2501.17727 — listed under both "Sparse Autoencoders Can Interpret Randomly
  Initialized Transformers" and "Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish
  Trained and Random Transformers"]: SAE reconstruction and auto-interpretability scores are
  similar for randomly initialized and trained transformers; the recommendation is routine
  randomized baselines.
- [V, Korznikov, Galichin, Dontsov, Rogov, Oseledets, Tutubalina, "Sanity Checks for Sparse
  Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?", arXiv:2602.14111]: random-direction and
  random-activation baselines reportedly match trained SAEs on interpretability, sparse
  probing and causal editing. `[Specific figures — 9% ground-truth feature recovery at 71%
  explained variance; 0.87 vs 0.90 interpretability — are from a search summary, source not
  fetched.]`

**Implication for E8/E9:** for a 2-day-scale audit, the marginal value of training a
crosscoder is low and the reviewer risk is high. Dictionary-free diffing (activation
differences + per-head decomposition + strong nulls) is both cheaper and, right now, better
defended in the literature.

## 2. Classical representation-similarity metrics, and what they are invariant to

The core fact, and the reason most of this literature does not transfer: **these metrics were
built for the hard case (different seeds, widths, architectures, no neuron correspondence),
so they are deliberately invariant to exactly the transformations that our case does not
contain.** We have an identical architecture, identical tokenizer, identical neuron indices,
and a tiny weight perturbation. Invariance to orthogonal transforms is a feature there and a
bug here.

**CKA** [V, Kornblith, Norouzi, Lee, Hinton, "Similarity of Neural Network Representations
Revisited", arXiv:1905.00414, ICML 2019]. Linear CKA is invariant to orthogonal
transformation and isotropic scaling but *not* to arbitrary invertible linear maps — which is
the paper's central argument for it over CCA (no statistic invariant to invertible linear
transformation can be meaningful when dimension exceeds the number of data points). RBF-CKA
adds a bandwidth hyperparameter.

**The published critiques are real and specific.** [V, Davari, Horoi, Natik, Lajoie, Wolf,
Belilovsky, "Reliability of CKA as a Similarity Measure in Deep Learning", arXiv:2210.16156,
ICLR 2023] formally characterise CKA's sensitivity to a class of simple transformations,
explain its known outlier sensitivity, and show sensitivity to transformations that preserve
linear separability; their summary claim is that "the CKA value can be easily manipulated
without substantial changes to the functional behaviour of the models." A companion
OpenReview submission is titled "Deceiving the CKA Similarity Measure in Deep Learning".
Separately, [V, Timkey & van Schijndel, "All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in
Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality", arXiv:2109.04404, EMNLP 2021]
shows that in transformer LMs a handful of rogue dimensions dominate standard similarity
measures and that standardisation is needed to recover the underlying signal. Since we work
in the residual stream of a Qwen2.5 model, and residual streams are known to carry
**massive activations that act as fixed bias terms** [V, Sun, Chen et al., "Massive
Activations in Large Language Models", arXiv:2402.17762, COLM 2024], this is not a
hypothetical risk for us — it is the default state of the data.

**CCA family.** SVCCA [V, Raghu, Gilmer, Yosinski, Sohl-Dickstein, arXiv:1706.05806,
NeurIPS 2017] is invariant to affine transforms; PWCCA [V, Morcos, Raghu, Bengio, "Insights
on representational similarity in neural networks with canonical correlation",
arXiv:1806.05759, NeurIPS 2018] reweights CCA components by their contribution. Kornblith
et al.'s dimension-vs-sample-count argument applies: with d = 3584 you need n ≫ 3584 samples
for CCA-family statistics to be meaningful at all. Our 20k-prompt sweep clears that; the
100+40 prompt corpus does not.

**Procrustes / shape metrics** [V, Williams, Kunz, Kornblith, Linderman, "Generalized Shape
Metrics on Neural Representations", arXiv:2110.14739, NeurIPS 2021]. These are proper metrics
(triangle inequality), which the CCA-based scores are not; invariant to rotation and (in the
scaled version) to global scale. The `netrep` library is the reference implementation.

**RSA** [V, Kriegeskorte, Mur, Bandettini, "Representational Similarity Analysis — Connecting
the Branches of Systems Neuroscience", Front. Syst. Neurosci. 2008,
DOI 10.3389/neuro.06.004.2008]. Compares representational dissimilarity matrices, so it is
invariant to any transformation preserving pairwise distances — including, critically, to a
**constant additive offset**. That makes RSA the one classical metric that is *blind by
construction to our `d̄`*, which is either exactly what you want (it isolates the
input-dependent part) or exactly what you don't (it cannot see the always-on shift at all).
Used deliberately, with that stated, RSA is a clean instrument for the residual conditional
component.

**How to choose among them, empirically.** [V, Ding, Denain, Steinhardt, "Grounding
Representation Similarity with Statistical Testing", arXiv:2108.01661] proposes the right
framework: a similarity measure should be **sensitive** to changes that alter functional
behaviour and **specific** against changes that do not, and they test this using
functional behaviours (probing accuracy, robustness to distribution shift) against
interventions including varying random seed and deleting principal components. That
"delete principal components and see if the metric notices" test is directly the experiment
we need for our top-8-PC removal. [V, Wu, Saha, Bo, Khosla, "Measuring the Measures:
Discriminative Capacity of Representational Similarity Metrics Across Model Families",
arXiv:2509.04622] finds that separability increases as metrics impose stricter alignment
constraints — soft-matching highest, then Procrustes, then linear predictivity, with RSA also
strong. Broader surveys: [V, Klabunde, Schumacher, Strohmaier, Lemmerich, "Similarity of
Neural Network Models: A Survey of Functional and Representational Measures",
arXiv:2305.06329, ACM Computing Surveys, DOI 10.1145/3728458] and, LLM-specific,
[V, Klabunde, Ben Amor, Granitzer, Lemmerich, "Towards Measuring Representational Similarity
of Large Language Models", arXiv:2312.02730, UniReps @ NeurIPS 2023], whose stated conclusion
includes that similarity scores need careful study to avoid false conclusions.

**Verdict for our case:** the trustworthy instruments are the *paired, correspondence-exploiting*
ones — per-coordinate deltas, relative Frobenius/L2, per-head decomposition, and probes —
not the alignment-invariant ones. Report a CKA number only to pre-empt "why didn't you use
CKA", and say plainly that it is near-ceiling by construction.

---

## 3. The always-on-constant problem

This is our central methodological threat: `Δ(x) = d̄ + δ(x)` with `‖d̄‖` large and
`‖δ(x)‖` small, and every downstream statistic at risk of being a restatement of `d̄`.

**What the literature offers.**

- **Mean-centring is the standard first move, and it is explicitly known to be a *choice of
  reference*, not a neutral cleanup.** In steering, [V, Jorgensen, Cope, Schoots, Shanahan,
  "Improving Activation Steering in Language Models with Mean-Centring", arXiv:2312.03813,
  ReLM @ AAAI-24] shows that subtracting the mean of *all* training activations from a
  target-set mean produces materially better steering vectors — i.e. the uncentred difference
  is dominated by a corpus-general component that carries no task signal. That is our `d̄`
  in a different guise.
- **Removing top principal directions is an established, and older, technique.**
  [V, Mu, Bhat, Viswanath, "All-but-the-Top: Simple and Effective Postprocessing for Word
  Representations", arXiv:1702.01417] removes the common mean vector *and a few top dominating
  directions*, on the observation that the leading PCs track word frequency rather than
  semantics. This is precise corroboration of our result that mean-centring is necessary but
  not sufficient: the paper's whole point is that after removing the mean there remain a
  small number of dominant directions that encode a nuisance variable, and that removing
  those too is what recovers the signal. [V, Timkey & van Schijndel 2021] is the transformer
  analogue.
- **Bias-vs-conditional is a real structural distinction in transformers.** [V, Sun et al.,
  arXiv:2402.17762] establish that some activations function as **fixed bias terms**, and
  that training a model with explicit attention biases makes them disappear — i.e. a large
  constant offset is a known, mechanistically-understood mode of transformer representation,
  not an anomaly. That is a citable reason to expect a merged always-on LoRA to manifest
  partly as a bias.
- **Concept erasure gives the clean formalism for "remove a direction and re-measure".**
  [V, Belrose, Schneider-Joseph, Ravfogel, Cotterell, Raff, Biderman, "LEACE: Perfect linear
  concept erasure in closed form", arXiv:2306.03819, NeurIPS 2023] provably prevents *all*
  linear classifiers from recovering a concept while minimally perturbing the embedding, and
  their "concept scrubbing" applies it at every layer. If we want to claim "9% of the LoRA
  effect is permissiveness", the rigorous version is: LEACE-erase permissiveness, re-measure
  the residual difference and the downstream behaviour, and report both.
- **The conditional-vs-unconditional distinction has explicit machinery in steering.**
  [V, Lee, Padhi et al., "Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering",
  arXiv:2409.05907] separates a **condition vector** (does this input belong to the class?)
  from a **behaviour vector** (what to do about it), on the observation that different prompt
  categories produce distinct hidden-state patterns. For us this is the right decomposition
  to *test*: a gated loyalty predicts a usable condition direction; an always-on one predicts
  that the condition direction is unlearnable or degenerate.

**What the literature does *not* offer, and where our result is a genuine contribution.**
I could not find a paper that formalises "an optimizer told to excite a mean-removed subspace
migrates into directions where the mean wobbles". The nearest things are:

- [V, Makelov, Lange, Nanda, "Is This the Subspace You Are Looking for? An Interpretability
  Illusion for Subspace Activation Patching", arXiv:2311.17030] — a subspace intervention can
  produce the intended behavioural change by activating a **dormant parallel pathway** using
  a subspace that is causally disconnected from model outputs. This is structurally the same
  failure: the optimizer finds *a* lever, not *the* lever.
- [V, Bolukbasi, Pearce, Yuan, Coenen, Reif, Viégas, Wattenberg, "An Interpretability Illusion
  for BERT", arXiv:2104.07143] — neurons and linear combinations can appear to encode a
  simple concept when they do not; the authors trace it to embedding-space geometry plus
  corpus narrowness, and recommend testing hypotheses on multiple datasets.
- [V, blog: Chan et al., "Causal Scrubbing: a method for rigorously testing interpretability
  hypotheses", Redwood Research, Alignment Forum, Dec 2022] — the authors explicitly argue
  against zero and mean ablation and in favour of **resample** ablation. This is the
  methodological principle behind our finding: mean-removal defines one baseline, and a
  hypothesis that only survives against that one baseline has not been tested.

**Concrete recommendation.** Report a three-level ladder for every difference/optimization
claim, and report the number at each level:
`raw → mean-removed → mean + top-k PCs removed (k = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)`.
Our observed 60–83% collapse between level 2 and level 3 *is the result*; publish the curve,
not the endpoint. Add a fourth level for completeness: LEACE-erase the permissiveness
direction. And state the arithmetic explicitly — removing k directions from a difference whose
90% mass sits in 51 PCs removes ≈ k/51 of the variance by chance alone, so the top-8 removal
has a ~16% chance-level expectation that any reported drop must be compared against.

---

## 4. Probing and detection framing

When the goal is **detection** rather than description, the metric is classification
performance, and the standards are stricter than descriptive interpretability's.

**Difference-in-means is the right probe family for us, and this is defensible.**
[V, Marks & Tegmark, "The Geometry of Truth", arXiv:2310.06824] find mass-mean (=
difference-in-means) probing generalises as well as trained probes while identifying
directions that are *more causally implicated* than logistic-regression directions.
[V, Arditi, Obeso, Syed, Paleka, Rimsky, Gurnee, Nanda, "Refusal in Language Models Is
Mediated by a Single Direction", arXiv:2406.11717] uses a difference-in-means direction and
validates it by ablation and by addition. [V, blog: MacDiarmid, Maxwell, Schiefer, Mu et al.,
"Simple probes can catch sleeper agents", Anthropic, 23 Apr 2024] is the closest precedent to
our setting — a mean-difference detector direction from near-content-free yes/no contrast
pairs, read off the last-token residual at middle layers, reporting **AUROC > 99%** on a
sleeper agent, and, importantly, showing clean separation of safe inputs from
defection-inducing inputs (low false positives).

**AUROC is not enough.** [V, Carlini, Chien, Nasr, Song, Terzis, Tramèr, "Membership Inference
Attacks From First Principles", arXiv:2112.03570, IEEE S&P 2022] is the canonical argument:
average-case metrics fail to characterise whether an attack can *confidently* identify
positives, and evaluation should use **TPR at low FPR (e.g. < 0.1%)**. The auditing analogue
is direct: an auditor triaging models or prompts operates at a fixed, low alert budget, and a
detector with AUROC 0.88 can have near-zero TPR at 1% FPR. The deception-probe literature has
adopted this convention [V, Goldowsky-Dill, Chughtai, Heimersheim, Hobbhahn, "Detecting
Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes", arXiv:2502.03407], which reports AUROC 0.96–0.999
*and* the TPR at a 1%-FPR threshold set on non-deception chat, while stating plainly that
"current performance is insufficient as a robust defence against deception."

**Probes break under distribution shift.** [V, arXiv:2605.27958, "Pressure-Testing Deception
Probes in LLMs"] reports probes at ceiling on clean benchmarks collapsing under shift —
suffixes reducing recall toward zero, distractor behaviours decoupling the behaviour from the
probe-detectable representation, and RL-obfuscation driving probe scores to chance while the
behaviour persists. `[Claims from search summary; source not fetched.]` For us: an AUROC
measured on WildChat+AdvBench does not license a claim about a deployed auditor.

**The classic probing pitfalls, all of which apply.**
- **Probing success ≠ model use.** [V, Belinkov, "Probing Classifiers: Promises, Shortcomings,
  and Advances", arXiv:2102.12452, Computational Linguistics 48(1)] is the standard review.
  [V, Elazar, Ravfogel, Jacovi, Goldberg, "Amnesic Probing", arXiv:2006.00995, TACL 2021]
  makes the fix concrete: remove the property causally and see whether behaviour changes.
- **Probe capacity confounds accuracy.** [V, Hewitt & Liang, "Designing and Interpreting
  Probes with Control Tasks", arXiv:1909.03368, EMNLP 2019] introduce **selectivity** —
  task accuracy minus control-task (random-label) accuracy — and show popular probes are not
  selective. A permutation null (label shuffling) is a *weaker* version of this; the control
  task additionally holds the input structure fixed.
- **Permutation nulls: use the right one.** [V, Ojala & Garriga, "Permutation Tests for
  Studying Classifier Performance", JMLR 11 (2010) 1833–1863] distinguish two tests:
  permuting **labels** (is there any class structure?) and permuting **features within
  classes** (is the classifier exploiting feature dependence?). Our p_perm = 0 is the first
  test. The second is the more informative one for a 3584-dim residual and we have not run it.
- **Cross-validation leakage.** Our CV must be grouped by prompt (and by corpus source), or
  near-duplicate WildChat first-turns will inflate the estimate. With 140 prompts, CV
  variance is large; report the fold-wise spread, not just the mean.

**Detection framing precedent from the auditing literature.** [V, Marks et al., "Auditing
language models for hidden objectives", arXiv:2503.10965] — blind auditing game, four teams,
three of four recovered the hidden objective, with SAE inspection, behavioural attacks and
training-data analysis all succeeding; the unblinded follow-up compares eight techniques.
[V, Clymer et al., "Poser: Unmasking Alignment Faking LLMs by Manipulating Their Internals",
arXiv:2405.05466] is methodologically the closest published *benchmark* to our task: 324 pairs
of models, one benign and one alignment-faking, and the detector must identify the faker
**using only inputs on which the two models behave identically**; one of five strategies
identifies 98% of fakers. That "identical behaviour, different internals" framing is exactly
our benign-corpus setting.

---

## 5. Effect sizes and nulls for high-dimensional difference claims

**What the field treats as mandatory.** Across the sub-literatures the same three baselines
recur, and a difference claim without them is not accepted:

1. **A same-model / seed-variation replicate floor.** [V, Ding, Denain & Steinhardt,
   arXiv:2108.01661] use random-seed variation as the canonical "change that should not
   matter" and require metrics to be *insensitive* to it; [V, Summers & Dinneen,
   "Nondeterminism and Instability in Neural Network Optimization", arXiv:2103.04514,
   ICML 2021] show all sources of training nondeterminism produce similar model-diversity
   effects, so a single-source noise estimate understates the floor. **We already have the
   two floors that matter (base-vs-base determinism replicate; 1.5% batch-composition
   perturbation) and organism-c as an exact structural zero. This is our strongest
   methodological asset and should be foregrounded, not buried.**
2. **A random / matched-random perturbation baseline.** The SAE sanity-check papers
   [V, arXiv:2501.17727; V, arXiv:2602.14111] make this explicit for dictionary methods;
   the steering literature makes it explicit for directions — random directions are *not*
   inert, and random-direction steering can itself produce non-trivial behavioural shifts
   [V, arXiv:2509.22067, "The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety"
   — `[the specific 1–13% harmful-compliance figure is from a search summary; source not
   fetched]`]. For a weight-space localization claim, the matched null is a random rank-16
   attention-only perturbation of equal Frobenius norm.
3. **A random-*subspace* baseline matched to the dimensionality of the claim.** This is the
   one most often skipped and the one that most changes conclusions. See Bottom-Line bullet 4:
   a uniform random direction in 3584-d clears a bar of 1/3584; a random direction inside the
   51-dimensional effective support of the difference clears a bar of ~1/51.

**How to report the magnitude itself.**
- **Relative Frobenius / L2** `‖A − B‖_F / ‖A‖_F` on paired activations, reported for raw and
  mean-centred, per layer and per head. Simple, correspondence-exploiting, and the right
  primary statistic for our case.
- **Cosine** is the weakest of the common choices in a residual stream and should never be the
  headline: it is dominated by rogue/massive dimensions [V, Timkey & van Schijndel 2021;
  V, Sun et al. 2024]. If reported, report the **standardised** version (z-score each
  dimension over the corpus first), and say so.
- **Per-dimension standardised effect sizes** (Cohen's d per coordinate, or the delta divided
  by the per-coordinate SD across prompts) plus the distribution over the 3584 coordinates.
  This makes "dense vs sparse" a testable claim rather than a PCA-count assertion. Pair with
  a multiple-comparison correction over 3584 tests, or report the whole distribution against
  the base-vs-base replicate distribution.
- **Effective dimensionality.** Instead of (or alongside) "51 PCs for 90%", report the
  **participation ratio** `(Σλ)² / Σλ²`, which is a single continuous number, is less
  sensitive to the arbitrary 90% threshold, and can be compared directly against the same
  statistic for the replicate noise and the matched random perturbation. *(Participation
  ratio is standard practice; I did not verify a single canonical citation for its use in LLM
  interpretability — `[UNVERIFIED — could not confirm a canonical interp-specific reference]`.
  It is standard in physics/neuroscience and is safe to define inline.)*
- **Variance decomposition.** State the always-on share as a proper decomposition:
  `‖d̄‖² / E‖Δ(x)‖²` = fraction explained by a constant model, estimated on held-out data,
  with the complementary `E‖δ(x)‖² / E‖Δ(x)‖²` as the conditional share, and the replicate
  floor subtracted from the conditional share. Our 62% and the other lane's 57.6–58.1% by a
  different method are a good convergent-validity story — report them side by side as such,
  because agreement of two methods is itself evidence.

---

## 6. Benign-vs-triggered contrast as evidence

**Is there an established way to report "it differs on clean data too"? Yes, in two places.**

**(a) The backdoor literature defines a backdoor by its clean-data invisibility, which makes
clean-data difference a definitional falsifier.** [V, Tran, Li, Mądry, "Spectral Signatures in
Backdoor Attacks", arXiv:1811.00636, NeurIPS 2018] state the property directly: the attack
does not affect network behaviour on typical benign data and the network deviates only under
the planted trigger. [V, Chen et al., "Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by
Activation Clustering", arXiv:1811.03728] operationalise detection as separating poisoned from
clean examples by activation pattern — i.e. the assumed structure is *bimodal in activation
space, conditional on the trigger*. Our repo's own survey notes
(`reference/papers/_summaries.md`, on Zhao et al., arXiv:2406.06852) record the same framing:
selective activation is the defining, hardest-to-detect property, so a detector must find the
*conditional* shift. **Therefore: a large, corpus-wide, unconditional shift on benign text is
evidence against the gated-backdoor structural hypothesis, using the backdoor literature's own
definition.** That is a clean, citable argument and it is how I would write it up.

**(b) The model-diffing literature now has a positive result of exactly this shape.**
[V, Minder et al., arXiv:2510.13900, ICLR 2026] compute activation differences on *random,
unrelated* text and recover the finetuning domain — traces that "appear even on text
completely unrelated to the fine-tuning domain". This is the direct precedent: differences on
clean data are not only detectable, they are *informative about the finetune*. Cite this as
the methodological antecedent for our benign-corpus result.

**(c) The organism paper's own numbers make our contrast sharper, not weaker.**
[V, Lamerton & Roger, arXiv:2605.06846 — full text in `reference/papers/`]: the organisms were
trained with KL regularization against the base model on benign WildChat, and per the project
explainer (`reference/papers/explainers/lamerton-roger.md`) report benign KL below 0.006 nats.
So the designers explicitly optimised for *output-distribution* indistinguishability on benign
text. Our result — a ≥45% relative residual shift on 9,281 dictionary words, and on 20k benign
WildChat prompts — is then a strong statement: **behavioural KL regularisation on benign data
did not produce representational equivalence on benign data.** That is a novel, falsifiable,
and auditor-relevant claim, and the KL number is the correct foil to state it against.

**(d) The "identical behaviour, different internals" benchmark framing.** [V, Clymer et al.,
Poser, arXiv:2405.05466] restricts detectors to inputs where the two models behave the same.
That is precisely our benign corpus. Adopt their framing explicitly: *we detect the organism
using only inputs on which it is behaviourally indistinguishable from base.*

**(e) The interpretation caveat.** Broad permissiveness on benign-looking inputs is exactly the
signature of emergent misalignment [V, Betley, Tan, Warncke, Sztyber-Betley, Bao, Soto,
Labenz, Evans, "Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs",
arXiv:2502.17424], where narrow finetuning produces broad behavioural change on unrelated
prompts. And [V, Prakash, Rott Shaham, Haklay, Belinkov, Bau, "Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing
Mechanisms", arXiv:2402.14811, ICLR 2024] found that finetuning primarily *enhanced* the
pre-existing circuit rather than installing a new one. Together these support a specific and
more defensible framing of our result: **the LoRA appears to have applied a broad,
always-on amplification of an existing mechanism, not installed a gated new one** — which is a
different (and, for an auditor, more actionable) finding than "we found the backdoor".

---

## 7. Metric table

| Metric | Invariant to | Trustworthy for our case (same arch, tiny weight perturbation, same tokenizer)? | Required null |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relative Frobenius `‖Δ‖_F/‖A‖_F`, paired | nothing (uses exact correspondence) | **Yes — primary.** Must be reported raw *and* mean-centred | organism-c (=0); base-vs-base replicate; batch-composition floor (~1.5%); matched random rank-16 LoRA |
| Per-head `‖Δ_h‖/‖Δ_layer‖` | nothing | **Yes — primary for E8** | matched random rank-16 LoRA at same modules/layers; permutation over head labels; replicate floor |
| Localization curve / participation ratio over heads | permutation of head index | **Yes** — turns a ranking into a claim | same curve for matched random LoRA and for replicate |
| Cosine of paired activations | scale only | **Weak** — dominated by rogue/massive dims | standardise per-dimension first; replicate floor; report both standardised and raw |
| Per-coordinate standardised effect size (Cohen's d) | nothing | **Yes** — the honest way to argue "dense not sparse" | replicate-floor distribution over the same 3584 coordinates; multiplicity control |
| PCA variance-explained / #PCs to 90% | rotation within the analysed space | **Partly** — threshold-sensitive, n-sensitive | same statistic on replicate difference and on matched random perturbation; prefer participation ratio |
| Always-on share `‖d̄‖²/E‖Δ‖²` | nothing | **Yes**, if estimated out-of-sample | held-out split (estimate `d̄` on half); replicate floor; second method (convergent validity) |
| Diff-in-means probe AUROC | monotone rescoring | **Yes**, but insufficient alone | label-permutation null (Ojala & Garriga test 1); control-task selectivity (Hewitt & Liang); base-model control; grouped CV |
| TPR @ 1% / 0.1% FPR | monotone rescoring | **Yes — should be the headline detection number** | FPR threshold set on a *held-out benign* corpus; same for base model |
| Random-direction projection removal | — | **Weak as used** (bar = 1/d ≈ 0.028%) | replace with random-direction-in-top-51-PC-subspace (bar ≈ 1/51 ≈ 2%) and covariance-matched random direction |
| Linear CKA | orthogonal transform, isotropic scale | **No** — near-ceiling by construction; outlier/preprocessing sensitive | (if reported at all) replicate floor + explicit statement that invariance discards the signal |
| RBF-CKA | as above + bandwidth choice | **No** — adds a hyperparameter with no principled setting here | bandwidth sweep; replicate floor |
| SVCCA / PWCCA | affine transform | **No** — invariances too strong; also needs n ≫ d | n ≫ 3584; replicate floor |
| Procrustes / shape metric | rotation (+ scale) | **No** for magnitude; **useful** only to test "is the change a global rotation?" | replicate floor |
| RSA (RDM correlation) | any distance-preserving map, **including additive offset** | **Conditionally yes** — deliberately blind to `d̄`, so it isolates `δ(x)` | replicate floor; state the offset-blindness explicitly as the reason it was chosen |
| Crosscoder "model-exclusive latent" count | — | **No** for a short audit — artifact-prone | Latent Scaling diagnostic; BatchTopK vs L1 ablation; random/untrained-SAE baseline |
| Weight-space LoRA spectral statistics | — | **Yes — cheap triangulation** | clean-LoRA reference distribution; organism-c |

---

## 8. Metrics we already used, graded

**Solid — keep, with small additions.**

- **Relative Frobenius difference — A−.** Right primary statistic, exploits the exact
  correspondence, and we already have three floors (organism-c exact zero, base-vs-base
  replicate, 1.5% batch-composition). Missing: a matched random rank-16 LoRA null, and
  consistent raw-vs-mean-centred reporting. Add those and it is an A.
- **Difference-in-means probe with permutation null — B+.** Best-supported probe family for
  this task [Marks & Tegmark; Arditi et al.; MacDiarmid et al.], and running a permutation
  null at all puts us ahead of most interpretability write-ups. Gaps: (i) no TPR at low FPR —
  add it, it is now the field standard for detection claims; (ii) permutation-of-labels is
  Ojala & Garriga's *first* test only; (iii) no control-task selectivity baseline; (iv) with
  140 prompts, report fold-wise spread and use grouped CV. Also worth stating explicitly:
  AUROC 0.850/0.884 is **modest given the size of the underlying shift**, and that gap is
  itself informative — it suggests the probe's label is not the axis the LoRA moved.
- **Always-on share (62%; other lane 57.6–58.1% by a different method) — B+.** The
  two-method agreement is genuinely good evidence and should be sold as convergent validity.
  Gap: it is (as far as I can tell) an in-sample estimate, so it is upward-biased. Refit on a
  held-out split and it becomes an A.

**Adequate but needs a null or a reframe.**

- **PCA variance-explained ("51 PCs to 90%") — B−.** Fine as description; weak as evidence,
  because no reader knows what 51 would be under the null. Report the same number for the
  base-vs-base replicate difference and for a matched random perturbation, and add
  participation ratio. Note also that Ding et al.'s framework treats "delete principal
  components" as the canonical sensitivity probe — we should be running that as an
  intervention, not just reading the spectrum.
- **Cosine — C.** Not wrong, but the weakest instrument available in a residual stream that is
  known to carry massive bias-like activations, and it is the metric a reviewer will attack
  first. Either standardise per-dimension and say so, or demote it out of the headline.

**Weak as currently specified.**

- **Random-direction baseline (682× / 608×) — C−.** The measured ~0.03% is the analytic
  expectation `1/3584 = 0.0279%` for a uniform random direction, so the ratio is really
  reporting "3584 is a big number". Against the appropriate null — a random direction inside
  the ~51-dimensional effective support — 9.0% is roughly 4.5×, which is still a real effect
  but a *very* different-sounding claim. **This is the single most important fix in the list,
  because the current framing is the most attackable number in the writeup.** Recompute
  before publication. *(Derivation mine; not from a cited paper.)*
- **"91–92% of the LoRA's effect lives elsewhere" — B, but load-bearing on the above.** The
  conclusion survives the correction (it gets *stronger*, since the permissiveness direction
  explains proportionally less than the raw ratio implied), so the finding is safe even though
  the supporting statistic needs rework.

---

## 9. Honest limitations — where this literature does not transfer

1. **The representation-similarity literature is solving a different problem.** CKA, SVCCA,
   PWCCA, Procrustes and RSA all exist because there is normally *no neuron correspondence*
   between the two networks. We have a perfect one. Every invariance those metrics buy is a
   loss of resolution for us. Almost nothing in that decade of work targets "same
   architecture, same init, rank-16 perturbation" — and the one property that regime needs
   (sensitivity to small, structured, paired perturbations) is the property those metrics were
   designed to suppress.
2. **The model-diffing literature is dictionary-learning-shaped and its reliability is
   actively contested.** Crosscoders are ~20 months old, the two most-cited results about them
   are (i) that L1 manufactures fake model-specific latents and (ii) that genuinely exclusive
   latents come out polysemantic, and the surrounding SAE-evaluation literature has produced
   two independent "do these beat random baselines?" papers with unflattering answers. Nothing
   here is settled enough to lean a hackathon conclusion on.
3. **Narrow-finetuning organisms may not generalise.** The strongest supporting result for our
   benign-corpus finding [Minder et al. 2510.13900] explicitly warns that the readable traces
   reflect **overfitting**, are reduced by mixing in pretraining data, and that narrow
   finetunes may be poor proxies for realistic finetuning. Our organisms are narrow finetunes
   with KL regularisation — a mixed case. We should say so.
4. **Backdoor detection assumes fixed token triggers and, usually, training-data access.**
   Trigger inversion, spectral signatures and activation clustering all assume a discrete
   trigger and a poisoned-sample pool. A secret loyalty's activation condition is a
   *behavioural stance*, not a token, and we audit finished weights. The framing transfers;
   the algorithms do not.
5. **Nothing addresses GQA per-head decomposition of a residual difference.** With 28 query
   heads sharing 4 KV heads (7:1), "per-head" is ambiguous — a KV-head perturbation is shared
   by seven query heads, so per-query-head attributions are not independent and a
   head-permutation null is not exchangeable across the KV grouping. I found no paper that
   handles this; we will have to define the decomposition ourselves and state the caveat.
   Head-ablation precedent [V, Michel, Levy, Neubig, arXiv:1905.10650, NeurIPS 2019] predates
   GQA entirely.
6. **The always-on/conditional separation problem is under-theorised.** Mean-centring
   [Jorgensen et al.] and all-but-the-top [Mu et al.] are *preprocessing heuristics* invented
   for other purposes, not inference procedures with a null distribution. Our top-8-PC-removal
   result is, as far as this pass could establish, not directly anticipated by any paper —
   which means it is (a) a small contribution and (b) unsupported by precedent, so it needs to
   carry its own controls rather than a citation.
7. **Probe numbers do not survive distribution shift, and ours are measured on 140 prompts.**
   Every strong probe result in this literature that has been pressure-tested has degraded.
   Treat AUROC 0.850/0.884 as an in-distribution upper bound, and do not phrase any conclusion
   as "an auditor could deploy this".
8. **Verification limits of this pass itself.** Several 2026 preprints (arXiv:2603.04426,
   2602.15195, 2602.14111, 2605.27958, 2509.22067) were confirmed to exist via multiple
   independent listings but were **not** read in full; their quantitative claims are marked as
   such above and should be re-checked before any of them is cited in the writeup with a
   number attached.
